title: StackSage onboarding feedback / activation + early retention
topics: What got StackSage to first value (first successful request)
Where they paused after initial testing (why they didn’t return)
Console onboarding nudges (helpful vs annoying, dismissal)
Docs/quickstart gaps and sample code requests
Model choice: quality vs cost vs latency tradeoffs
Next steps to re-activate and define success criteria for a pilot
summary: StackSage shared candid feedback on Redwood Hosted API onboarding. They reached first value quickly using the TypeScript SDK + a minimal “hello world” snippet and streaming, but paused after initial tests because they didn’t have a clear path from “it works” to “production confidence”: evals/regression checks, cost predictability, and a simple checklist for going from first request → 100k tokens → first feature shipped. They also noted mild friction around API key handling across environments and wanted clearer guidance on rate limits and what “good” looks like for TTFT/latency. Email onboarding was mostly helpful, but one teammate never received the second email (possible deliverability/suppression). Console nudges were useful when contextual (API key creation / first request), but they asked for less repetition after dismissal. Redwood will follow up with a short activation checklist, recommended model + settings for their use case, and a 2-week pilot plan with success metrics and instrumentation.
action_items: Jordan Blake - Send StackSage a 2-week pilot plan outline (success criteria, milestones: first request, 100k tokens, D7 active) by 2026-01-30
Dylan Brooks - Share a minimal chat example + streaming snippet aligned to StackSage’s Node/TypeScript stack by 2026-01-30
Nikhil Sharma - Recommend a default model + parameters for their support-agent summarization flow (quality vs cost) and share guidance on structured output by 2026-02-03
Jordan Blake - Loop in Marketing Ops to investigate why Miguel didn’t receive email #2 (suppression / deliverability) by 2026-02-03
Asha Patel - Confirm their target latency + monthly token expectations and whether they need any data retention constraints by 2026-02-04
next_steps: Redwood to email a short “Activation checklist” and pilot plan
StackSage to re-run tests with streaming + recommended model/settings and aim to cross 100k tokens in the next 7 days
Schedule a 30-min technical deep dive on evals/monitoring and cost predictability (token accounting, caching/batching guidance)
Confirm whether StackSage wants to stay Hosted API for pilot or discuss Dedicated capacity
transcript:
Fireflies.ai transcript

Meeting: StackSage onboarding feedback / activation + early retention
Date: 2026-01-29
Time: 10:30 AM - 11:11 AM (PT)
Duration: 41 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood), Dylan Brooks (Redwood), Nikhil Sharma (Redwood), Asha Patel (StackSage), Miguel Santos (StackSage)

---

[Auto-summary]
- StackSage got to first request quickly with TS SDK + hello-world snippet; streaming helped perceived speed.
- They paused after “it works” due to uncertainty on production readiness: evals, regression, cost predictability, and what steps come next.
- Console nudges were helpful early but became repetitive; dismissal persistence needs to stick.
- One user missed an onboarding email; possible suppression/deliverability issue.
- Next steps: pilot plan, model/settings recommendation, example app, and follow-up deep dive.

---

[00:00] Jordan Blake: Cool. Hey Asha, Miguel—thanks for making time. This one’s pretty informal. We’re doing a bunch of activation and early retention work on the Hosted API, and we wanted feedback from folks that actually tried to wire it up, then… you know, either shipped or didn’t.

[00:16] Asha Patel: Yeah, makes sense. Happy to be candid.

[00:18] Miguel Santos: Same. And sorry if I’m like, slightly late, I was finishing a deploy.

[00:23] Jordan Blake: No worries. Dylan is here from our console/tooling side, and Nikhil from product for Hosted API.

[00:30] Dylan Brooks: Hey.

[00:31] Nikhil Sharma: Hi both.

[00:34] Jordan Blake: Maybe we start with context. What were you trying to do when you signed up? Like what’s the use case, and what did “first value” look like?

[00:45] Asha Patel: We’re building a sort of support-agent assist inside StackSage. We ingest internal tickets, some docs, and then propose a response draft and a summary. We wanted something we could control for latency and cost, and we didn’t want to go all-in on one proprietary API.

[01:05] Miguel Santos: Specifically we were testing like, “summarize this thread, propose next reply,” plus a classification like sentiment and category. So a mix of generation and some structured bits.

[01:20] Jordan Blake: Got it. And how quickly did you get to a first successful request?

[01:25] Miguel Santos: Pretty quick, actually. I used the TypeScript SDK. The docs had the snippet—like the hello world. It was basically copy/paste, set REDWOOD_API_KEY, call the chat endpoint.

[01:38] Dylan Brooks: Nice.

[01:40] Miguel Santos: The one thing that helped a lot was the streaming example. Like, I don’t know if it truly changes the total latency, but it made it feel fast because tokens show up.

[01:52] Nikhil Sharma: Yeah, perceived TTFT matters. Do you remember if you had any hangups before that first request?

[02:00] Miguel Santos: Minor. The first hangup was my own fault—I had an API key in my local shell but then my dev server runs in a different env. So I got “missing API key” and I was like… why is it not picking it up. But the error message was decent.

[02:15] Asha Patel: For me, the console flow was fine. Create key, then there was a little checklist thing? I don’t know if it was new but it said something like “make your first request.”

[02:26] Dylan Brooks: That’s probably one of the nudges we’re testing. Was it helpful or annoying?

[02:31] Asha Patel: Helpful in the sense it pointed me to the right page. But later I kept seeing it and I thought I dismissed it.

[02:39] Dylan Brooks: Oh. That’s useful. It’s supposed to persist dismissal per user.

[02:43] Miguel Santos: Yeah I saw that too. Like it came back when I switched pages.

[02:46] Dylan Brooks: Okay, that might be the “wrong page” state—sorry. We have a bug in some edge cases where it re-renders and forgets the dismissal.

[02:56] Jordan Blake: Cool, we’ll take that. So you got to first value quickly. What made it feel like value? Just “I saw output,” or did you run it on real data?

[03:05] Miguel Santos: I ran it on a handful of real ticket threads. The summaries were good. Not perfect, but usable.

[03:11] Asha Patel: We also looked at the usage dashboard. That was good because I could sanity check tokens and cost. Like, “okay it’s not insane.”

[03:22] Jordan Blake: Great. So where did you pause? Because from our side, we saw the account was active for like two days and then kind of flat.

[03:31] Asha Patel: Yeah. Two things. One is: once it works, the next question is “now what?” Like, how do we go from a few manual calls to confidence it won’t regress, and it won’t blow up our spend.

[03:47] Miguel Santos: Exactly. We didn’t have an eval harness set up. And we’re comparing a couple providers. We tried OpenAI and Anthropic before. With them, we have like, a bunch of internal wrappers already. With Redwood we were like, okay this is promising, but we’d have to do some of that work again.

[04:05] Nikhil Sharma: When you say eval harness, do you mean like prompt tests and regression alerts, or something else?

[04:10] Miguel Santos: Yeah, like a set of 50 example tickets and expected-ish outputs. Doesn’t have to be exact, but like scoring. Also structured output compliance. We tried to force JSON and sometimes it’s… you know.

[04:25] Nikhil Sharma: Makes sense. We do have structured output guidance and tool calling patterns, but we might not be surfacing it early enough.

[04:33] Asha Patel: The other big reason we paused is cost predictability. Like, we can see token usage per request, but we didn’t know what the “right” model choice is for our workload. We picked one from the catalog, but it wasn’t obvious if we should go smaller and accept some quality loss.

[04:52] Jordan Blake: Which model did you start with?

[04:54] Miguel Santos: I think it was… “Llama something 70B”? Or maybe 8B. I might be mixing it up.

[05:02] Nikhil Sharma: That’s okay. We can look after. In general, for summarization and drafts, a strong 8B or 14B can be enough depending on your prompt.

[05:13] Asha Patel: And then there’s latency. For the agent assist, we need it to feel instant. Like sub-second to first token would be ideal. We got close sometimes, but other times it was like… two seconds before anything.

[05:29] Dylan Brooks: Two seconds TTFT, or total time?

[05:31] Asha Patel: Time to first token.

[05:34] Dylan Brooks: Okay. That’s a big lever. Streaming helps hide it, but we should still lower it. Were you testing from the west coast, or where?

[05:42] Miguel Santos: Mostly US west, yeah.

[05:45] Jordan Blake: One thing we’re doing in this sprint is making the onboarding path explicit: sign up → create key → first request → streaming → usage dashboard → “first 100k tokens.” Did you even notice the 100k token milestone?

[05:58] Asha Patel: No. That’s… that’s the first I’m hearing it.

[06:02] Miguel Santos: Same.

[06:04] Jordan Blake: That’s helpful feedback. We’re using it internally as a proxy for “you did more than toy usage.” But if it’s not visible, it doesn’t motivate.

[06:12] Dylan Brooks: We have a nudge planned for that but it might not be on for your cohort.

[06:17] Asha Patel: I’d love a checklist that’s not just “make a request.” Like: “here’s how to choose a model, here’s how to set max tokens, here’s how to watch for costs, here’s how to evaluate quality.”

[06:31] Nikhil Sharma: Totally. The “what next” after hello world.

[06:35] Miguel Santos: Also rate limits. We got one error that looked like a rate limit, and I wasn’t sure if it’s per-minute or concurrency. It wasn’t a blocker, but it’s one of those things where you’re like, “okay if we ship this, what happens?”

[06:49] Jordan Blake: That’s fair. Hosted API has default quotas. We can increase, and Dedicated exists when you need predictable throughput. But early on, we should explain the defaults clearly.

[07:03] Dylan Brooks: Do you remember the exact error message?

[07:05] Miguel Santos: Not exact. Something like “too many requests” or “quota exceeded.” Could have been me spamming it.

[07:13] Dylan Brooks: Okay.

[07:14] Jordan Blake: Switching gears—email onboarding. Did you get emails from us? Helpful? Too many? None?

[07:21] Asha Patel: I got the welcome email. Then one about streaming, I think. That one was useful because it linked to the docs.

[07:30] Miguel Santos: I got the first one and then… I didn’t get the second. I thought maybe I unsubscribed accidentally, but I don’t think so.

[07:38] Jordan Blake: Interesting. That might be suppression logic or deliverability. We’ve been ramping volumes and trying to be conservative.

[07:46] Asha Patel: Also, small thing: the subject lines felt a bit marketing-y. Like “Ship faster” whatever. But the content inside was pretty dev-focused so it was fine.

[07:55] Jordan Blake: That’s good to know. We’re trying to keep it developer-first.

[07:59] Nikhil Sharma: Was there anything you wished the emails covered that they didn’t?

[08:04] Asha Patel: The “what next” again. Like a short path to production confidence.

[08:10] Miguel Santos: Yeah. And a link to a minimal example repo. Not a huge framework. Just “here’s a tiny chat app, here’s how to set env vars, here’s streaming.”

[08:22] Dylan Brooks: We do have a minimal template. I can send that.

[08:25] Jordan Blake: We’ll send it after.

[08:28] Jordan Blake: Can I ask, what would have made you come back on day 7? Like what signal would have pulled you back in?

[08:36] Asha Patel: If we had a clear recommendation on the model and cost. Like “for your use case, start here, expect X cost per 1k tickets,” and “here’s how to measure it.”

[08:49] Miguel Santos: And honestly, if we had a little nudge in console saying “run this on 20 real tickets and compare,” with a button that links to an eval script.

[09:00] Nikhil Sharma: That’s a good idea. We have Redwood Optimize and some eval tooling, but the self-serve surface isn’t super cohesive yet.

[09:10] Dylan Brooks: When you were in console, what did you look at most?

[09:13] Asha Patel: Usage and keys. I didn’t click much else.

[09:18] Miguel Santos: I looked for logs. Like request logs. I found something but it wasn’t super detailed.

[09:25] Dylan Brooks: Yeah, request tracing is limited on self-serve right now unless you add headers for correlation. We can show you how.

[09:33] Jordan Blake: You mentioned comparing providers. Where does Redwood stand today relative to OpenAI/Anthropic for you?

[09:40] Asha Patel: Quality: for our summarization, it was comparable enough on a small sample. Speed felt okay, not always. The main differentiator for us is: can we get predictable economics and not be locked in.

[09:56] Miguel Santos: Also data. Some of our customers ask about data retention. With OpenAI, we have to explain stuff. With you, we didn’t get far enough to understand what’s stored and for how long.

[10:07] Jordan Blake: Good callout. Hosted API has standard logging for operational purposes, but we have options and Private/VPC for regulated. For self-serve onboarding, we probably need a clearer “data handling at a glance” link.

[10:20] Nikhil Sharma: For your current pilot, do you have any hard constraints? Like “no prompts stored,” or “EU only,” or anything.

[10:27] Asha Patel: Not yet. Some customers are EU, but we’re not at the point of promising residency. For now we just want to know what we can say.

[10:36] Jordan Blake: Makes sense.

[10:38] Dylan Brooks: Back to the nudges. You said you dismissed but it came back. Were there any nudges that were actually helpful beyond API key creation?

[10:46] Asha Patel: The one that linked to streaming was good.

[10:50] Miguel Santos: Yeah, and one that said “view usage dashboard” was fine. But if I’ve already clicked it, it shouldn’t keep showing.

[10:58] Dylan Brooks: Totally.

[11:00] Jordan Blake: What about friction points in the docs? Any missing step that cost you time?

[11:06] Miguel Santos: The docs were okay. The main gap was around structured output. Like, there’s “you can do structured output,” but not like a definitive recipe with pitfalls.

[11:18] Nikhil Sharma: That’s fair. We can send a recipe: strict JSON schema, retry-on-parse-fail, and a few prompt patterns.

[11:27] Asha Patel: Also, clarity on default timeouts and retries. Our wrapper needs to know if the SDK retries automatically.

[11:35] Dylan Brooks: In the TS SDK, we don’t do aggressive retries by default for generation, mostly because it can duplicate cost. But we can point you to recommended patterns.

[11:47] Jordan Blake: Helpful. I want to make sure we capture “why churn.” It sounds less like “this didn’t work,” and more like “we hit the cliff after the first dopamine hit,” right?

[11:59] Asha Patel: Exactly. Like, you got us to “cool, output.” Then we didn’t have the next rung.

[12:05] Miguel Santos: And we got busy. So without a clear plan, it just sits.

[12:10] Jordan Blake: That’s the honest reality.

[12:12] Nikhil Sharma: If we gave you a 2-week plan with milestones—run on X tickets, evaluate outputs, track cost, pick model—would that be enough to re-engage?

[12:23] Asha Patel: Yes. If it’s short and concrete.

[12:26] Miguel Santos: And if there’s code, I’ll do it.

[12:30] Dylan Brooks: Great.

[12:31] Jordan Blake: Let’s talk about your throughput expectations. Roughly how many tickets per day would you run through this if shipped?

[12:38] Asha Patel: In early beta, maybe 2,000 tickets/day. If we roll out, maybe 20k/day. Each ticket could be a few thousand tokens including context.

[12:50] Jordan Blake: Okay. That’s meaningful but not insane. Hosted can handle it, but we’d want to ensure quotas and latency.

[12:58] Miguel Santos: One question: do you support embeddings too? We didn’t test that.

[13:03] Nikhil Sharma: Yes, embeddings endpoint. For your use case, you might do retrieval on docs. We can recommend models.

[13:10] Asha Patel: We already have embeddings with another provider. Switching is work.

[13:14] Jordan Blake: Understood.

[13:16] Dylan Brooks: On latency variability, did you notice it tied to time of day?

[13:20] Miguel Santos: Hard to say. It was like, sometimes first token is quick, sometimes slow. We only tested a few times.

[13:29] Dylan Brooks: Okay.

[13:30] Jordan Blake: Another thing we’re experimenting with is “first 100k tokens in 7 days.” Would a progress bar in console help, or is that gimmicky?

[13:39] Asha Patel: If it’s tied to something meaningful, sure. Like, “you’re 80% to unlocking higher quota,” or “unlock a consult,” or something.

[13:48] Miguel Santos: Yeah, gamification is fine if it maps to real stuff.

[13:52] Jordan Blake: Got it.

[13:53] Nikhil Sharma: Any feedback on the API itself? Anything weird, naming, response shape?

[13:58] Miguel Santos: It was fine. We like that it looks like other APIs. The only annoyance is we had to map message roles. That’s normal.

[14:08] Asha Patel: The one thing: the usage dashboard shows tokens but I didn’t see a breakdown per route or per environment. Maybe we didn’t tag it.

[14:17] Dylan Brooks: You can pass metadata tags—like “environment: staging.” It’s not super obvious in onboarding.

[14:23] Asha Patel: That would help.

[14:25] Jordan Blake: Cool, we’ll include that in follow-up.

[14:28] Jordan Blake: Switching to retention: what would make you trust it enough to ship?

[14:33] Asha Patel: Two things: (1) quality doesn’t regress unexpectedly—so some guardrails, and (2) latency is stable. If it spikes randomly, our agents will hate it.

[14:45] Miguel Santos: Also, a path to Dedicated if we need it, without rewriting everything.

[14:51] Jordan Blake: That’s exactly our thesis. Same API surface, different deployment mode.

[14:56] Dylan Brooks: On the console side, we can set alerts if activation drops, but for your product, you’d want alerts on latency and error rate. We can show you dashboards.

[15:07] Asha Patel: Yeah.

[15:09] Jordan Blake: Okay. Let me recap what I heard, and you tell me if I’m missing something.

[15:13] Jordan Blake: You got to first value quickly with TS SDK + streaming. You paused because you need a clearer “what next” plan: model choice guidance, cost predictability, eval harness, and a checklist to go from test → pilot → shipped feature. Emails were generally helpful but Miguel missed one. Console nudges were helpful early but the dismissal persistence and repetition needs work.

[15:41] Asha Patel: That’s accurate.

[15:43] Miguel Santos: Yep.

[15:44] Jordan Blake: Awesome. Here’s what we’ll do. I’ll send a 2-week pilot plan with concrete steps and success metrics. Dylan will send a minimal example repo and the streaming snippet. Nikhil will recommend a model and settings for summarization + draft replies and share structured output recipes.

[16:03] Nikhil Sharma: And we can hop on a short technical session about evals and how to track quality. Like a lightweight approach.

[16:11] Asha Patel: That would be great.

[16:13] Miguel Santos: Yep, I’ll join.

[16:15] Jordan Blake: Last question—are you okay if we follow up with a couple more onboarding emails? We’re testing sequences.

[16:21] Asha Patel: Yes, as long as it’s actually technical.

[16:24] Miguel Santos: If I get them.

[16:26] Jordan Blake: (laughs) Fair. We’ll investigate. Anything else you want to add before we drop?

[16:33] Asha Patel: Just—don’t hide the “production path.” That’s the big one.

[16:38] Miguel Santos: And fix the nudge coming back. That one was mildly annoying.

[16:42] Dylan Brooks: Noted.

[16:44] Jordan Blake: Cool. Thanks both. We’ll follow up by end of day tomorrow with the materials and scheduling.

[16:50] Asha Patel: Sounds good.

[16:51] Miguel Santos: Thanks.

[Meeting ended]
